parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A stationary wave is formed on a string XY that has a length of $0.48\text{ m}$. Fig. 5.1 shows the string at one instant in time.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The speed of the wave on the string is $1400\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, draw a cross $(\times)$ at one position that is a node and another cross at one position that is an antinode. Label the node N and the antinode A.

markscheme_points.text: cross labelled N marked at the intersection of the solid and dashed lines or at X or Y and cross labelled A marked at a peak or a trough

hints: Hint 1: Think about where the string never moves at all compared to where it swings up and down the most - look for where the wave crosses the dashed rest position versus where it reaches a crest or trough.
parts.proper_answer: N at X or Y or at either crossing of solid and dashed lines. A at a crest or trough (maximum displacement).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Stays Still and What Moves Most**
Imagine the string vibrating up and down. A node is a point that stays at zero displacement all the time. An antinode is a point that oscillates with largest amplitude. On the diagram the dashed line is the rest position.

Step 2: **Pick the Spots**
Where the solid wave meets the dashed line the displacement is zero - that is a node. This happens at X, at Y, and at the two places in between. Mark N at any one of those. Where the wave is highest or lowest - the top of a hump or bottom of a dip - the motion is biggest. Mark A at any one of those peaks or troughs.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the wavelength of the wave produced is $0.32\text{ m}$. Explain your reasoning.

markscheme_points.text: (XY is 1.5 wavelengths, so) wavelength = 0.48 x (2 / 3) = 0.32 m or (wavelength is twice node-node distance so) λ / 2 = 0.48 / 3 = 0.16 m and wavelength = 0.16 x 2 = 0.32 m

hints: Hint 1: Count how many half-wavelength segments fit into the 0.48 m length by looking at the number of node-to-node gaps, or count full sine waves from X to Y.
parts.proper_answer: Length XY contains 1.5 wavelengths, so $\lambda = 0.48/1.5 = 0.32\text{ m}$. Equivalently node-node distance $= 0.48/3 = 0.16\text{ m} = \lambda/2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Count Wavelengths in the String**
Look from X to Y. You see one full hump up, one full dip down, then another hump up but the pattern ends at Y. That is one and a half complete waves. So $$0.48\text{ m} = 1.5\lambda$$

Step 2: **Do the Division**
Rearranging gives $$\lambda = \frac{0.48}{1.5} = 0.32\text{ m}$$ Another way to see it: there are three node-to-node gaps in 0.48 m, each gap is $\lambda/2$, so $\lambda/2 = 0.16\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the wave.
hints: Hint 1: Recall which universal link connects wave speed, frequency and wavelength for a travelling wave, and note that the stationary pattern is made from travelling waves with the same speed.
Hint 2: Check you have $v = 1400\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda = 0.32\text{ m}$ in SI units, then rearrange to make frequency the subject before substituting.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the Wave Equation**
For any wave the speed is how many wavelengths pass per second: $$v = f\lambda$$ Here $v = 1400\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is given and you just found $\lambda = 0.32\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Calculate the Frequency**
Make $f$ the subject: $$f = \frac{v}{\lambda}$$ Then substitute: $$f = \frac{1400}{0.32} = 4375\text{ Hz} \approx 4400\text{ Hz}$$ Give 2 s.f. to match the data.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A source of sound waves of frequency $780\text{ Hz}$ is on a rotating platform. The speed of the source is $39\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The sound is detected by an observer that is a large distance from the rotating platform, as shown in Fig. 5.2.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

Fig. 5.2 (not to scale)
parts.text:
The speed of sound in air is $320\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate the maximum frequency of the sound detected by the observer.
hints: Hint 1: Think about when the detected pitch is highest during the rotation - it is when the source velocity component directly towards the distant observer is largest.

Hint 2: Recall how the observed frequency depends on $f_s$, $v$ and $v_s$ for a source moving towards a stationary observer, and decide whether to use $v - v_s$ or $v + v_s$ in the denominator for the maximum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Condition for Maximum**
The observer is far away so only the line-of-sight speed matters. The observed wavelength is shortened when the source chases its own sound waves. Highest frequency happens when the source moves straight towards the observer at full speed $v_s = 39\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Apply the Doppler Formula**
For a source approaching a stationary observer: $$f_o = f_s \frac{v}{v - v_s}$$ Substitute $f_s = 780\text{ Hz}$, $v = 320\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $$f_o = 780 \times \frac{320}{320 - 39} = 780 \times \frac{320}{281} \approx 888\text{ Hz} \approx 890\text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
At time $t = 0$, the observer detects the sound emitted by the source when it was in the position shown in Fig. 5.2.

On Fig. 5.3, sketch the variation with $t$ of the frequency $f$ of the sound detected by the observer for one complete rotation of the platform. Calculations are not required.

{{figure:figure_5_3}}

Fig. 5.3

markscheme_points.text: line showing f varying both above and below a mean frequency and returning to the original start value of f
a single cycle of a smoothly oscillating curve of correct phase (starting at mean position, falling to a trough, then rising to a peak, ending at mean position)

hints: Hint 1: Start by working out the line-of-sight speed in the position shown - the motion arrow is at right angles to the direction to the observer, so is the observed frequency high, low or equal to 780 Hz at $t = 0$?
Hint 2: Think about what happens just after $t = 0$ as the source swings round - does it start to move away from or towards the observer, and how will $f$ vary smoothly over one full circle?
parts.proper_answer: Smooth sine-like curve starting at $f = 780\text{ Hz}$ at $t=0$, falling first to a minimum, then rising through mean to a maximum, then returning to mean at end of one rotation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Starting Point**
At the instant shown the source is on the right side moving up. Its velocity is across the line to the distant observer, so the component towards the observer is zero. That means no shift at $t = 0$, so start your curve at the mean source frequency $f = 780\text{ Hz}$.

Step 2: **Follow One Rotation**
Just after this instant the source moves round to the back of the circle, away from the observer. Wavelengths are stretched so $f$ falls to a minimum. Half a rotation later it comes round the front moving straight towards the observer, so $f$ rises to a maximum. The variation of line-of-sight speed is sinusoidal, so draw one full smooth wave: start at mean, dip down, come up through mean to a peak, then back to mean.
